Tort law is the area of law which addresses civil wrongs that harm others, regardless of whether any agreement exists between the parties. In contrast, contracts protect only parties who have agreed to be bound by the agreement, whereas torts protect parties who have not.
Tort law defines what constitutes a legal injury and establishes the circumstances under which one person may be held liable for another's injury. The purpose of tort law is to provide relief for victims who have been injured through the carelessness of others. Compensation for the harm they have suffered comes from the responsible party, rather than from the government or from the victim's own assets or insurance contracts.
Tort cases may arise when a person's reasonable expectations are not met as a result of another party's negligence, or when a party breaches a duty not to commit a civil wrong. The injured party may sue for damages to compensate for the harm suffered. Some damages are quantifiable (e.g., medical expenses, lost earnings), while others are more subjective (eantertainment value of a vacation). Tort law also provides for punitive damages, intended to punish the defendant for particularly egregious behavior, and to discourage others from similar conduct.
The term "tort" comes from Latin, where it has the meaning of "wrong". Its first known appearance in the English language dates to 1580.
Tort law has been established over centuries, starting with the old English law of trespass, while the modern development of tort law began in the mid-19-century.

In tort law, strict liability is the doctrine that makes a person responsible for the harm caused by their actions and products even if the person was not negligent or otherwise at fault. It is generally applied to cases involving abnormally dangerous activities, products liability, wild animals, and trespass to land.
The concept of strict liability, where one party is held legally accountable for the consequences of their actions without regard to culpability, is an aspect of tort law that has been developed by the courts over several centuries.
The concept of strict liability actually originated in the area of criminal law in the early 19 century. It was introduced to discourage people from dealing in explosives, which were considered to be inherently dangerous.
The courts of England and the United States adopted the concept in relation to activities that posed a public hazard, such as the keeping of wild animals and the storage of explosives. In the case of wild animals, it was held that the defendant would be liable even if they took all possible care.
A similar rule was applied to the keeping of explosives, which were held to be so dangerous that the owner would be liable even if they took all possible care in storing them. The defendant would also be liable if they intended to use the explosives for lawful purposes, but the explosives were stolen and then used to cause damage.
The concept of strict liability was later extended to the area of civil law, where it was applied to cases involving products that were considered to be inherently dangerous, such as explosives and poisons.
The rule of strict liability for products was first articulated in the early 1906 case of Rylands v. Fletcher, in which the defendant had been held liable for the escape of water from his reservoir onto the plaintiff's land. The court held that the defendant would be liable if he had collected and kept something on his land that was not necessary for his use, and which might do mischief if it escaped. The rule was later modified in several cases to cover only those products that were inherently dangerous, and that would not cause damage if they were used as intended.

The Texas Maternal Mortality and Morbidity Task Force is set to expire in January unless lawmakers take action, putting crucial strategies to protect mothers and infants at risk.
The task force is an important tool to examine the underlying causes of maternal mortality, in order to provide the best solutions for policies and practices to prevent these deaths.
The role of the task force is to analyze each pregnancy-associated death. By reviewing individual cases, the task force brings together physicians, nurses, epidemiologists, and public health experts who can help determine whether a death can be attributed to pregnancy, including any factors that might have contributed. By examining the underlying causes of maternal deaths, the task force ensures that the state can identify the best ways to reduce the number of deaths.
The Texas task force was created by the Legislature in 2013. In 2014, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) developed new standards for death certificates, allowing for improved reporting of pregnancy-related deaths.
Since then, the task force has been able to extend its work due to federal funding. But the funding expires in January. Unless lawmakers take action, the task force will end its work.
The task force’s early analysis found that Black women accounted for about one in nine births in Texas but nearly three in ten maternal deaths. The task force brought together experts to determine why and to provide solutions. Research showed that the gaps in access to care for Black women in Texas and throughout the country have contributed to this disproportionate rate of death among Black women.
According to the task force, increasing access to the full spectrum of health care is critical. Without adequate prenatal care, women are more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes. For example, access to comprehensive care can identify or treat conditions that could harm women and their infants if left untreated.
The task force’s work has also found that the deaths of women in Texas are not only caused by pregnancy complications but also by other factors that arise. According to the Texas task force, women who are unable to obtain comprehensive healthcare due to barriers such as high co-payments or lack of insurance are particularly vulnerable.
The task force’s extension will help policymakers identify gaps and develop solutions to these challenges and to increase access to care for Texas women.
The federal government provides block grant funding to the state in order to help pay for the task force. By extending its work, Texas could continue to receive this funding. The task force’s work will help researchers identify and prevent the causes of maternal mortality, an important marker of a country’s overall health that reflects its health infrastructure.
A look at state and local efforts to address maternal mortality further underscores the importance of the Texas task force. In 2020, Texas would have been the first state to lose its Medicaid funding from the federal government under the “Block grant” plan, which would have cut $50 billion from the federal government over the next 10 years. This plan would have cut funding for Medicaid, which would have limited access to prenatal healthcare, which has been shown to increase maternal mortality rates.
In a 2020 study by Erica L. Eliason, it was found that cutting Medicaid funding limits access to prenatal healthcare, which has been shown to increase maternal mortality rates. In addition to identifying pregnancy-related deaths, CDC’s definition of pregnancy-related deaths extends the period to one year from the resolution of the pregnancy. The CDC definition includes deaths of women who have had a live birth, stillbirth, or miscarriage, as well as deaths of women who are known to be pregnant, and those who are believed to be pregnant but are not confirmed.
The CDC does not require death certificates to include “pregnant” or “pregnant at time of death,” but it does require the cause of death to be pregnancy-related. The CDC definition also includes indirect obstetric deaths, which are caused by pregnancy interfering with or worsening an existing condition, such as a heart problem.

Natural resources

The researchers link this protection to the pre-existing type I interferon response.
